note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 3083 / 出力 2150 トークン

data.interpretation: The KPI asks to maximize the number of orders delivered within the promised pickup and delivery times across the whole town, so the primary metric is on_time_deliveries. The promised times (DELIVERY_SLA) may be revised, but 'on time' is defined by the SLA itself. Loosening the SLA can raise on_time_deliveries without customers getting their orders any sooner. To measure the effect on customers, SLA-independent metrics are needed: the order-to-delivery wait times (p95_wait_s, max_wait_s) and unfinished orders. The KPI states no numeric levels, so no targets or guard values are set.

options.label: On-time count as primary, with SLA-independent customer-impact monitors

goals.text: Number of orders delivered within the promised pickup and delivery times, town-wide (maximize).
95th-percentile order-to-delivery wait time, town-wide. It does not depend on the SLA, so it shows whether customers actually wait longer after a change.
Longest order-to-delivery wait in the town. Monitored so a change cannot hide very long waits for a few customers.
Orders still undelivered at the end of the period. Monitored so no improvement comes from leaving orders undelivered.

options.note: Recommended. This is the direct reading of 'as many orders as possible within the promised times'. The wait-time monitors give the human the measured customer effect that the KPI requires before accepting any change that is worse for customers, such as a looser SLA. No guard values are set because the KPI gives no levels.

options.label: On-time count as primary, monitoring only SLA-relative outcomes

goals.text: Number of orders delivered within the promised times, town-wide (maximize).
Orders still undelivered at the end of the period (minimize).

options.note: A literal reading that judges everything against the current promises. It is simpler, but every metric here moves when the SLA is redefined. An SLA loosening would look like a pure improvement, with no measurement of how much longer customers actually wait.

options.label: Actual customer wait as primary, on-time count monitored

goals.text: 95th-percentile order-to-delivery wait time, town-wide (minimize). This cannot be improved by changing the promises.
Number of orders delivered within the promised times (monitored, should not drop).
Orders still undelivered at the end of the period (monitored).

options.note: Robust against SLA gaming, but it shifts the main objective away from the KPI's stated goal of counting on-time deliveries. Use it only if the human considers actual speed to be the true intent.

concerns: on_time_deliveries is a proxy defined by the SLA itself. Because the KPI allows revising promised times, loosening the SLA can raise the on-time count while customers wait just as long or longer. SLA-independent wait metrics should be measured alongside it.

The KPI requires that a change worse for customers be justified after measuring its effect, but it does not say which measure defines 'worse for customers'. Candidates are p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished. The human should confirm which one or ones apply.

The KPI gives no numeric levels (e.g., a minimum on-time count or a maximum acceptable wait), so no targets or guards were set. If hard limits on customer wait are intended, the human should state them.
SLA changes are contract-layer amendments. Customers do not vote, so any SLA revision must be decided by a human, using the measured wait-time effects.
The KPI is town-wide and says nothing about fairness between companies A, B and C. If one company's on-time rate collapsing is unacceptable, that should be stated explicitly.
